brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to Social Selling Techniques

questions.question: According to the course, what are the two axes that make up the Social Style framework?
choices: Personality and behavior
Ask versus Tell, and Task versus People
Emotion and control
Speed and accuracy
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly right—the entire model rests on those two questions: how does this person get what they want (Ask vs. Tell), and what drives their behavior (Task vs. People).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The framework is built on two specific questions about observable behavior. Review Slide 5 to see how the two axes—Ask versus Tell on the X axis, and Task versus People on the Y axis—create the foundation of the model.

questions.question: What is the signature question that Drivers tend to lead with?
choices: How?
Why?
What?
Who?
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—Drivers ask "What?" because they focus on results, outcomes, and what they get from a decision.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not the Driver's signature. Remember, Drivers are all about outcomes and speed, so their question focuses on what the result will be. Check Slide 11 for the full breakdown of all four signature questions.

questions.question: Which style is described as telling and task-focused?
choices: Analytical
Expressive
Driver
Amiable
questions.feedback_correct: Yes—Drivers tell and are task-focused, which puts them in the tell/task quadrant of the grid.
questions.feedback_incorrect: That's not the right combination. Drivers are the ones who tell (give direction, state opinions, push forward) and focus on tasks (outcomes, efficiency, data). Review Slide 6 to see all four styles plotted on the grid.

questions.question: What does low emotion and asking many questions typically signal about a customer's style?
choices: Driver
Analytical
Expressive
Amiable
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—an Analytical asks a lot of questions, moves methodically, and runs low on visible emotion, which separates them from the warm, high-emotion styles.
questions.feedback_incorrect: That combination points to a different style. Both task-focused styles (Driver and Analytical) run low on emotion, but the Analytical is the one who asks questions—they're methodical and laser-focused on accuracy and data. See Slide 9.

questions.question: What is a pressure behavior for an Amiable customer?
choices: Asking for more data and time
Taking control of the meeting
Becoming argumentative
Going quiet and withdrawing
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—when an Amiable feels pushed, misunderstood, or out of control, they tend to go quiet and withdraw rather than push back directly.
questions.feedback_incorrect: That's a pressure behavior for a different style. Each style reacts differently when the conversation goes off track. Amiables, who are relationship-focused and conflict-averse, tend to withdraw quietly. Review Slide 12 for the pressure behavior of each style.

questions.question: When selling to an Analytical, what should you prioritize in your discovery process?
choices: Building rapport and demonstrating enthusiasm
Highlighting who else is using your solution
Preparing detailed, logical questions and using evidence throughout
Focusing on their personal dreams and ambitions
questions.feedback_correct: Spot on—Analyticals need to feel that the process is rigorous, so detailed questions, evidence, and data throughout are essential to earn their trust.
questions.feedback_incorrect: That approach works for a different style. Analyticals are methodical and data-driven, and they hate being caught unprepared. They need logical questions, evidence, and time to evaluate—not enthusiasm or vision. See Slide 16 for the Analytical selling tactics.

questions.question: What does the course mean by a customer having an "adjacent" style?
choices: A style they learn over time through experience
A secondary style that sits next to their primary style and softens how it shows up
A backup style they use when under pressure
A style that is opposite to their primary style on the grid
questions.feedback_correct: Right—the adjacent style is the quadrant next to the primary one on the grid, and it modifies how the primary style actually behaves in real situations.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. An adjacent style is not learned or used only under pressure—it's a secondary influence that naturally softens or shapes the primary style. For example, a Driver with an Expressive adjacent will be more warm and conversational than a pure Driver. See Slide 13.

questions.question: How should you address a style mismatch once you notice it in a live conversation?
choices: Acknowledge what is happening, slow down, and shift your approach
Maintain your current approach and adjust after the meeting
Ask the customer directly what style they prefer
Switch immediately to a completely different selling strategy
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—when you catch a pressure behavior or drop in engagement, that's your signal to slow down, acknowledge what happened, and shift your approach to recover the rapport.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Early intervention is key. If you notice a pressure behavior or loss of engagement, you still have time to recover the relationship by shifting your approach. Waiting until after the meeting or making sudden major changes will not serve you. Review Slide 22 for how to spot and respond to mismatches early.

questions.question: When selling to an Amiable, why is it important to explain how you got to this meeting and who introduced you?
choices: It shows you have done your research thoroughly
It establishes authority and credibility with data
It provides the relationship context that matters to them because relationships are their currency
It demonstrates speed and efficiency in your process
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—Amiables are relationship-focused, and that introduction context signals trust, collaboration, and a human connection before diving into business.
questions.feedback_incorrect: That's not what matters most to an Amiable. While research and efficiency are good, Amiables prioritize relationships and safety. Explaining how you were introduced gives them the relational context they need to feel confident moving forward. See Slide 18.

questions.question: What is the relationship between your own Social Style and selling effectiveness across different customer styles?
choices: Your own style does not matter as long as you know the customer's style
You should try to match the customer's style by changing your personality
Your natural defaults may land differently with different customers, so awareness and deliberate adjustment are necessary
Only Drivers and Analyticals need to adjust their style; Expressives and Amiables are naturally versatile
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—your own style is part of the equation. What works naturally for you might shut down a customer with a different style, so conscious awareness and adjustment are the key to versatility.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Your own style absolutely affects how your approach lands with different customers. A Driver's direct, fast-paced approach works great with other Drivers but can alienate an Amiable. Review Slide 19 to understand why self-awareness is step one in developing versatility.
